title: Integration Is Signed Geometry
notes: Open with the idea that integration on a manifold is not merely a way to add local densities. It is a sign-sensitive construction. The same numerical magnitude can change sign when a frame is flipped, a chart reverses orientation, or a boundary normal is chosen inconsistently. The flow diagram gives the lecture map: determinants define positive frames, top forms test those frames, atlases globalize the choice, boundaries inherit a convention, and Stokes ties interior and boundary signs together.

title: Roadmap: Four Sign Checkpoints
notes: Use this slide as the explicit contract for the lecture. Students should hear that there are four sign checkpoints, and each one has a simple local test. A frame is compared by a determinant, a chart overlap is compared by the determinant of its transition Jacobian, a boundary is oriented by placing an outward vector first, and an integral changes by the signed Jacobian under pullback. The later examples are not separate tricks; they are repeated uses of these four checks.

title: Orientation Of A Vector Space
notes: Begin at the linear algebra level because every later manifold definition is pointwise. The formula u equals v times A should be read as a comparison between two ordered frames. If the determinant of A is positive, a continuous motion through invertible frames can carry one to the other without crossing singularity. If the determinant is negative, the frame has crossed to the opposite component. The chapter check gives concrete numbers, so this is not only an abstract equivalence relation.

title: Top Covectors Detect Orientation
notes: Move from frames to forms by emphasizing that a top covector is a measuring device with a sign. In two dimensions, dx wedge dy is the familiar signed area form, but the definition is dimension independent. A positive frame is exactly one on which the chosen top covector evaluates positively. This is the bridge to integration: a top-degree form is locally a signed volume element, so its integral must remember which frames count as positive.

title: Orientations On Manifolds
notes: Now globalize the linear picture. An orientation on a manifold is not one basis chosen forever; tangent spaces change from point to point. The smoothness condition says the choice of positive component is locally represented by smooth frames, or equivalently by a nowhere-zero top form. This is also where students should separate orientability from a particular orientation: orientability means such a smooth choice exists, while an orientation is one of the possible choices.

title: Oriented Atlases
notes: This slide translates orientation into coordinates. A chart gives an ordered coordinate frame, and an oriented atlas is one where all overlap maps compare those frames by positive determinants. Emphasize that the determinant belongs to the transition map, not to the manifold by itself. The point is compatibility: when two charts describe the same tangent frame, they must not disagree about which side of determinant zero they occupy.

title: Mobius Sign-Cycle Obstruction
notes: Use the Mobius band as the first global obstruction. Locally everything looks fine, so this is not a failure of charts or tangent spaces. The problem appears after transport around a loop: the twist returns a frame with the opposite sign. The check file records transition signs plus, plus, minus, whose product is minus one. That product is the compact witness that no oriented atlas can be chosen around the cycle.

title: Manifolds With Boundary
notes: Introduce boundary through the model space H to the n. This is deliberately local: a manifold with boundary is still n dimensional, but some points have neighborhoods that include only one side of a coordinate hyperplane. The last coordinate plays a special role in the local model, and that role is what later creates the outward normal. Keep the distinction sharp: the boundary is not a lower-dimensional manifold attached from outside; it is detected by the half-space charts of the original manifold.

title: Boundary Is Intrinsic
notes: This is the conceptual pause after the definition. Students may worry that boundary status depends on the chosen half-space coordinate. The theorem says it does not: if one chart sees the point on the edge, compatible charts must also see it on their edge. This makes the notation partial M legitimate. Once that is granted, the boundary can be treated as its own lower-dimensional manifold, which is necessary before Stokes can even be stated.

title: Boundary Orientation
notes: This is the sign convention students will use every time Stokes appears. The boundary orientation is created by contracting the ambient top form with an outward vector. Equivalently, a boundary frame is positive precisely when putting the outward vector in front gives a positive ambient frame. In the upper half-plane example, the outward vector is negative partial y, and contraction of dx wedge dy gives dx, so the bottom boundary points to the right.

title: Domains Of Integration
notes: This slide is a short analytic interlude. Before integrating forms on a manifold, the chapter needs ordinary integration over acceptable coordinate domains. The disk grid shows the reason a boundary of measure zero is harmless: the ambiguous cells live near the boundary, and their total area shrinks as the grid is refined. This prepares students for chart-based integrals, where the local domain may have a rough boundary but still supports a well-defined integral.

title: Signed Pullbacks
notes: Here the determinant sign directly changes an integral. The pullback formula for a top form is the cleanest way to say it: the coefficient is the determinant of the Jacobian, not its magnitude. The ellipse example is useful because the geometric region is unchanged. Only the parametrization has been reflected, and the integral flips from pi a b to negative pi a b. This reinforces the distinction between unsigned area and integration of oriented forms.

title: Integration Via Charts
notes: This slide states the manifold integral in the operational form students can use. A compactly supported top form is cut by a partition of unity, each piece is moved into coordinates by an oriented chart, and the resulting Euclidean integrals are added. The important point is independence from the auxiliary choices. Oriented chart changes preserve sign, and partition of unity refinements add to one, so the global number is not tied to a particular cover.

title: Stokes Theorem
notes: State Stokes as the climax of the chapter. The exterior derivative raises degree by one, so an n-dimensional integral of d omega is compared to an integral of omega over the n minus one dimensional boundary through the inclusion i from partial M into M. The sign convention is not optional: the boundary orientation from the previous slide is exactly what makes the local half-space calculation agree with the theorem. Present the proof roadmap rather than a full proof, highlighting partitions of unity and the normal direction.

title: Stokes In Calculus
notes: Connect the abstract theorem to familiar calculus without changing the sign story. For a gradient field, Stokes in one dimension is the fundamental theorem for line integrals: the oriented boundary of an interval is endpoint minus start point. In the plane, Green's theorem is Stokes for the one-form P dx plus Q dy. The counterclockwise boundary orientation and the dx dy area orientation are paired; reversing one would reverse the equality.

title: Sphere Area And Recap
notes: Close with the sphere because it feels familiar while still using the chapter machinery. The parametrization pulls the sphere area form back to the coefficient sine phi, and the double integral gives four pi. The example also lets you recap the sign arc in a concrete setting: choose an orientation, choose parameter order, pull back the form, and integrate. The final takeaway is that orientation is not extra decoration; it is the structure that lets local signed calculations assemble into global theorems.
